Do not hand-compute 637 `--ceiling` for a task gate — that is how twenty measured task gates 638 recorded ceilings of 1, 2, 6, and 7, two of which the cap makes 639 impossible. `--consumed` cannot express them. 640 3. **A spent cap is BLOCKED, not a gate round.** When the task's consumed 641 rounds already total five, `--consumed 5` yields a ceiling of zero and 642 the gate backstops on its first call. That is the fail-closed floor, not 643 the intended path: check before calling, and when the cap is spent follow 644 the breaker below and surface the task as BLOCKED rather than spending a 645 gate invocation to learn it. 646 647 The invariant in one line: **local gate rounds + non-gate fix rounds ≤ 5**, 648 enforced because `gate-round` blocks (verdict `backstop`) the moment its 649 local count would exceed the ceiling. Count every round the 650 gate runs against the task's shared budget — each gate round consumes one 651 of the five, exactly like a reviewer round. After a Codex-triggered fix, 652 the scoped re-review verifies it; the gate re-runs only once that 653 re-review verdicts every finding ADDRESSED or DECLINED. 654 655 **The breaker.** When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the 656 spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching. The task 657 does not silently continue and nothing is parked on your own authority: 658 surface the open findings to your human partner as BLOCKED, each with the 659 rounds already spent, what was tried, and the evidence. Ledger it: 660 `Task : BLOCKED at cap — `. They decide what happens 661 next. 662 663 ### 5. Complete the task 664 665 When the review comes back clean — the task reviewer approved, every 666 fix-loop finding is addressed or declined, and the per-task Codex gate 667 approved or was skipped by tier — in this order, each step idempotent on a 668 resume: 669 670 - Append `Task : approved ` with the head the reviewers saw, 671 written with `git rev-parse ` (every later approval of the same task 672 appends a new line; the newest is what merges). merge-back compares the 673 whole id, so a shortened id reads as no approval. 674 - Merge back: `scripts/sdd-state merge-back PLAN_FILE N --session --commit `. 675 `merged` continues (`already=1` on a resume means the ref was moved 676 before the crash). `conflict paths=`: merge the integration branch 677 into the task branch in your worktree (`git merge `), resolve 678 through one implementer dispatch whose brief names the paths and both 679 sides, re-run the task reviewer over the resolution and the task gate's 680 re-review lens, append the new `approved` line, and retry. `checked-out` 681 names a worktree or `lease:`: a final train holds the branch; post a 682 `tasks` record and retry after it ends, or ask your human partner to move 683 the checkout. `not-approved approved=` means your bookkeeping 684 is behind: the commit you passed is not the task's newest `approved` line, 685 so append the `approved` line for the head the reviewers saw (or pass that 686 head) and retry. `blocked waiting=` (exit 7) means an amendment put a 687 prerequisite under your claim after you took it, and merge-back enforces 688 the edge: leave the `approved` line as it is, and never write a completion 689 line for a task this session did not complete. Run `next` and take what it 690 offers; on `own-blocked`, post, print the board and hand back as the 691 `own-blocked` text above says. Retry merge-back once every waiting task has 692 its completion line, or after your human partner removes the edge. 693 `not-holder owner=` (exit 4) 694 means the claim is no longer yours (after a takeover your human partner 695 granted, that session holds it): stop and hand back with the line; never 696 repair the ledger or take the claim back. 697 - Detach at the merged head and drop the task branch: 698 `git switch --detach ` then `git branch -d ` 699 (its commits are on the integration branch now; a missing branch on a 700 resume is fine). If `-d` refuses, the branch holds commits that were never 701 approved or merged: keep it, do not force the delete, and hand back to 702 your human partner with git's output. 703 - Complete the task: run `scripts/sdd-state complete PLAN_FILE N 704 --commits ..` and repeat it until it prints `status=complete` 705 (`busy` and `error` are retried; `unknown-task` means the number is not a 706 heading in the plan, `no-workspace` that the ledger is gone, and a usage 707 error that the arguments are wrong: each of those stops you, not the loop). 708 Its `snapshot=` is the completion's durable record. 709 - Mark the todo complete (where you keep todos), and run `next`. 710 711 A task whose ledger has a `merged` line and no completion line is resumed 712 at the completion line, never redispatched. 713 714 ## The waiting board 715 716 Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an 717 empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what 718 you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --kind 719 [--task N] --note ""`, and put 720 the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write. 721 When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --clear`. 722 The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among 723 several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet 724 after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt. 725 726 ## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability) 727 728 Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task 729 skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the 730 plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger 731 fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An 732 unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown — 733 executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and 734 records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final 735 whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write 736 `tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the 737 final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the 738 fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in 739 [risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared 740 low. 741 742 ## Final Review 743 744 The final train is claimed. When `next` says `complete`, run 745 `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE final --session `: `claimed` means 746 this session runs the final review, the final gate and Finish; `blocked` 747 names tasks still open (claims without completion lines elsewhere: wait or 748 ask); `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after compaction) 749 means this session already holds the train: continue as its holder; `held` 750 names the session that holds it, or `lease= plan=` 751 when a sibling plan's final holds the branch: post a `tasks` record naming 752 the holder, print the board, and hand back. The holder checks the 753 integration branch out in its own worktree (`git switch `), the 754 one time a session does so, and runs the review package, the final 755 reviewer, the fix wave and the final Codex gate on it; its fix commits land 756 on the integration branch directly, which the lease makes safe. 757 758 Once you hold the train and have checked the integration branch out, the 759 final whole-branch review gets a package too: run 760 `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the 761 branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) — take the path from the 762 `wrote : ...` line and include it in the final review dispatch, so the 763 final reviewer reads one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git 764 commands. Dispatch 765 on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using 766 hyperpowers:requesting-code-review's 767 [code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at 768 the ledger's deferred-minor lines — and at `tier-skips.md`, if any task 769 skipped its per-task gate — so it can triage which must be fixed before 770 merge. 771 772 If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent 773 with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding. Compose the 774 dispatch from [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md). 775 Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real 776 session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined. 777 Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave 778 (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range, 779 [re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) using its Final-wave usage note). 780 There is no second fix wave: anything the re-review leaves open — and any 781 finding that conflicts with the plan's text — goes to your human partner 782 with the evidence, as BLOCKED, when finishing-a-development-branch presents 783 the options. 784 785 **Dispatch the decision extractor.** When the ledger has a `Decisions listing:` 786 line (and otherwise nothing), once the fix wave and its re-review are 787 clean (or the final review returned no findings), take a scratch directory 788 from `../requesting-code-review/scripts/codex-review-dir`, regenerate the 789 full-branch package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`, so a 790 fix wave's commits are in it) and copy it and `/progress.md` into 791 it, and dispatch the 792 extractor in the background, composed from 793 `../finishing-a-development-branch/decision-notes-prompt.md` with those two 794 copies, the plan, the spec, the `Decisions listing:` from the ledger, the 795 index (`decisions/README.md` beside the spec's directory) when it exists, and 796 `/decision-notes.md` as its output path. Record it in the ledger: 797 `Decision extractor: -> /decision-notes.md`. The dispatch is 798 complete only when that line is in the ledger: write it before any other tool 799 call, because after a compaction it is the only record of the task id and the 800 notes path, and without it a resumed controller can neither collect nor stop 801 the extractor. The extractor reads nothing inside the workspace, so Finish may 802 delete the workspace while it runs; 803 finishing-a-development-branch collects it after the full suite and never 804 waits for it, and neither do you. On a harness with no tracked background 805 subagent, skip the dispatch and note it in the ledger. If a Codex final-gate 806 fix changes code after the dispatch: stop the extractor (TaskStop); when the 807 fix altered one of the spec's decisions, settle that first (show your human 808 partner the change you would write into the `## Decisions` item, write and 809 commit it on the branch with their approval; without it the item stands and 810 the change is raised again at the menu); re-run the dry run and replace the 811 ledger's `Decisions listing:`; regenerate the full-branch package and copy 812 it, with the current `/progress.md`, into the scratch directory, 813 replacing the earlier copies; compose the replacement dispatch from those 814 copies; then dispatch the extractor again and replace the 815 `Decision extractor:` line. 816 817 **Codex Review Gate — final whole-branch (Claude Code only).** After the final code-reviewer 818 subagent and its fix wave, and before hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, 819 run the gate using the final whole-branch code recipe with `--base `. Provide the branch 821 review-package path, plan or requirements path, the Minor findings ledger if 822 present, and the tier-skip summary if any task skipped. The final dossier passes the plan's `**Spec:**` file as a `--doc` input beside the plan, and carries the tier-skip summary among its `--adjudications`. Resolve blocking 823 findings with one fix subagent carrying the complete list, per this 824 section's existing guidance, before finishing. After any Codex-triggered 825 final-review fix, re-run the final code-reviewer before re-running the final 826 Codex gate. 827 828 Unlike the per-task gate, the final gate keeps a ceiling of its own: the 829 gate's convergence stop-rule and per-gate backstop bound this loop (code 830 gates use a code-gate backstop of 3 rounds). If the backstop is hit with 831 unresolved blocking findings, surface them to your human partner rather than 832 looping. 833 834 ## Finish 835 836 When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged: 837 838 1. **Read your session line** from the ledger (its `mode`), and copy the 839 ledger's `Decisions listing:` and `Decision extractor:` lines (or its 840 skip reason) into the hand-off message you are about to send: the next 841 step removes the ledger from the working tree, and 842 hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch takes the mode, the plan, the 843 spec and the extractor's task id and output path as its input. 844 2. **Finish the workspace** with `scripts/sdd-state finish PLAN_FILE --session `: 845 it refuses with `open-claims` while any claimed task lacks a completion line 846 (that is a plan not finished, not a reason for `--force`), and with 847 `busy` (exit 3) when another session is writing the workspace or a copy 848 from an interrupted removal sits beside it (report the stderr line, wait 849 for the other session or ask your human partner about the copy, then run 850 `finish` again); it also refuses with `live-jobs` while a tracked job it 851 names is still live (run `tracked-job wait` on it, or `tracked-job stop` 852 when the job is no longer wanted, then run `finish` again). `not-holder` 853 or `no-final-claim` (exit 11): this session does not hold the final 854 train; stop and hand back. Otherwise it 855 removes the plan's directory, commits the removal to the state branch, 856 and prints `last=`, the commit that still holds the dossier, 857 `push=/` and `receipt=`, the durable copy of the 858 ledger, the guard's log and the job records; record the receipt path in 859 your closing message. A line reading `receipt=none staging=` means 860 the record exists only under that staging path: name the path to your 861 human partner in the closing message. A space in either path prints as 862 `%20`, so decode it before you name the path. On the plain backend it 863 prints `backend=plain` instead of `last=` and `push=`, and there is 864 nothing to push. `none` means there was no workspace to remove, and 865 `error` (exit 2) that the removal or its commit failed: any status other 866 than `finished` stops Finish until the command 867 succeeds; show its stderr line. 868 3. **Verify deletion** with `test ! -d ""` to confirm it is gone. 869 The push command is `git -C push `, the 870 checkout being the parent of the `plans/` directory `sdd-dir` printed; 871 run it only if your human partner asks. 872 4. **Keep the lease through the branch action.** `finish` leaves the branch 873 lease in place; hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch marks the 874 branch closing before a merge and releases the lease after whichever 875 option your human partner chose. Hand it the plan path and your session 876 id for that. When the final ends with a hand-back instead, detach your 877 worktree first (`git switch --detach`) and then release the lease 878 yourself, as the last action: 879 `scripts/sdd-state lease PLAN_FILE --release --session `. 880 881 A clean finish that leaves the workspace behind is an INCOMPLETE finish — 882 "keeping it for reference" is not an option; the repo's commits are the 883 durable record. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them 884 alone. `scripts/sdd-state prune --repo ` is the only other remover, and it 885 runs only when asked. 886 887 Use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, passing the mode from your 888 session line. Hand it the plan and the spec, and the extractor's task id 889 and output path when one was dispatched; when the dispatch was skipped, 890 hand over the ledger's reason instead and say so, and finishing compiles 891 without notes; when the plan has no spec, say that, and finishing runs its 892 test-only path. A decision a Codex-gate fix altered was settled in Final 893 Review before the re-dispatch. 894 895 ## Common Rationalizations 896 897 The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true: 898 [common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you 899 catch yourself justifying a shortcut. 900 901 ## Example Workflow 902 903 A complete worked run, dispatch through finish: 904 [example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md). 905

## Setup Read before you settle: run the `sync` and `sdd-dir` steps below and read the ledger's plan line, if the ledger exists (reading it changes nothing). Then settle where the work happens: use hyperpowers:using-git-worktrees, which detects an existing worktree or asks your human partner to choose between staying on the current branch, a new branch in place, and a worktree, and reports the mode. When the plan line names an integration branch, this is a later session of a running plan: hand using-git-worktrees that branch and your session id. Never start implementation on a main/master branch unless your human partner chose "stay on the current branch" in that question; that answer is the consent, and the dossier no longer depends on the branch. Conversation memory does not survive compaction. In real sessions, controllers that lost their place have re-dispatched entire completed task sequences — the single most expensive failure observed. Track progress in a ledger file, not only in todos. - Each plan owns a workspace: at skill start, run `scripts/sdd-state sync PLAN_FILE` (it fetches the repository's state branch; outcomes below), then this skill's `scripts/sdd-dir PLAN_FILE` — it prints the plan's workspace inside the repository's state checkout under the user cache (`${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/hyperpowers/state//plans/-/`, one checkout per clone, shared by every worktree of it), home to every artifact for THIS plan: ledger, briefs, reports, review packages, claims, tier-skip summary. The ledger, reports, notes and claims are committed to the orphan branch `hyperpowers/state` by `scripts/sdd-state snapshot PLAN_FILE` and travel between hosts with that branch; briefs and review packages are ignored there and regenerate. The cache is off any protected path, so writing there never triggers a permission prompt, and it is outside the working tree, so it can never be committed with the code. Another plan's directory is never yours to read or write. When `sdd-dir` reports `backend=plain` on stderr, the state branch is unavailable on this host and the dossier will not travel from it: tell your human partner once and continue. - `sdd-state sync` outcomes: `up-to-date`, `fast-forwarded`, `merged`, `ahead`, `created`, `absent`, `no-remote`, `assumed-absent`, `plain`: continue. `offline` (exit 1): continue on the local checkout and, as soon as the ledger exists (the next bullet), append `state: sync offline at ` to it. `offline-no-state` (exit 1), or `needs-sync` from `sdd-dir`: stop; this host has no dossier and cannot learn whether the remote holds one. Ask your human partner to get online, or to confirm `scripts/sdd-state sync --assume-absent PLAN_FILE` when they know no remote dossier exists. `diverged` (exit 3): stop and present both tips and the printed `merge=` command as a question in the Deciding Together shape; never merge on your own. `busy` (exit 3): retry `sync` once after the other session's writes settle, then ask. `foreign` (exit 2): the branch at the state name is not a hyperpowers state branch; stop, relay the stderr remedy (set git config `hyperpowers.stateBranch` to another name), and ask. `remote-finished plans=` (exit 3): another host finished a plan whose workspace on this host holds ledger lines that are not on the branch. When the list names this plan's workspace, stop, show your human partner the lines this host added (the ledger's tail beyond the last snapshot), and ask whether to snapshot them (then `sync` again, which reports `diverged` for their merge) or to discard them. A workspace in the list that is not this plan's belongs to another plan: report its name and stop without reading or changing it. Any other status, `status=error` (exit 2) among them, stops the run until `sync` succeeds; show its stderr line. - Check for this plan's ledger at `/progress.md` — this plan's workspace only, never a sibling's. The workspace is the plan's identity: `scripts/sdd-dir` maps a plan to ONE directory whatever path form you hand it, so a ledger sitting in YOUR workspace is this plan's progress even when its first line records the path in another form. Compare repo-relative paths: reduce the plan you were handed to its path relative to the plan repository's toplevel; a line holding an absolute path matches when it lies inside this repository and reduces to the same relative path, or, when it names a path that does not exist on this host (a ledger written on another machine), when it ends with that relative path. Tasks with a `Task : complete` line are DONE — do not re-dispatch them; resume at the first task without one. A task whose last line is a fix round is mid-loop: resume the loop at the next round. A task whose last line is its implementer identity is a dispatch in flight: do not re-dispatch — reconcile that agent first (list your live children, chase its report), resume it by the recorded id where your harness allows, and only if it cannot be recovered dispatch a takeover, recording the takeover's identity beside the original. The scan only reads: every action it calls for (a resume, a takeover, the next task) waits until `verify` below has returned `ok`. A first line that resolves to a genuinely different plan file means this workspace is corrupt, not that you wandered into a sibling's: stop and surface it to your human partner rather than starting fresh on top of another plan's state. - When there is no ledger, create it with its identity as the first line, `# SDD ledger — plan: ` (never an absolute path: the ledger travels between hosts), through a no-clobber write so two sessions that both saw no ledger cannot overwrite each other: `( set -o noclobber; printf '# SDD ledger — plan: %s\n' > /progress.md )`. When that write fails because the file now exists, another session created it first: continue as if you had found it. Whether you created it or found one, append your session line (with `>>`, never a rewrite): `session : mode on integrating at started `, where `` is `$CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` on Claude Code and, on a harness without one, a value you generate once as `$(date -u +%s)-$RANDOM$RANDOM`, and the mode is what using-git-worktrees reported. Append a fresh session line whenever you move to a new task branch or detach; your newest line is your location. When your human partner assigned this session specific tasks, add `session : tasks `. Then, once registered (the next bullet), run `scripts/sdd-state verify PLAN_FILE` (on a found ledger this is the check that this host holds the code it relies on): `ok` continues; anything else stops Setup until `verify` passes again. `code-missing` names commits the ledger relies on that this checkout lacks, so ask your human partner to pull the named branch; `wrong-repo` names the repository the ledger was handed off from, so ask which checkout this work belongs in; `plan-stale` names the plan repository branch to pull, and you read the plan again after that pull. - Register the plan before anything else is claimed: `scripts/sdd-state register PLAN_FILE --session --integration `, where `` is the branch the branch choice produced (the plan's integration branch; later sessions read it from the ledger's plan line and pass the same). `registered` continues; `wrong-branch` means this plan is already running on another integration branch: switch to it or ask; `spec-branch-mismatch` means a sibling plan of this spec runs on another branch: use that branch; `branch-closing` means the plan's branch is being merged and deleted: wait for your human partner; `detached-head` (exit 11) means a first registration found the repository the line names on a detached HEAD, as a host-managed workspace can be, and the plan ref is named after a branch: ask your human partner for the branch to create (the integration branch itself when plan and code share one repository), create it in place with `git -C switch -c `, and register again. Any other status stops Setup until `register` succeeds; show its stderr line. A later session of a running plan starts its worktree detached at the integration head (using-git-worktrees says how) and never checks the integration branch out; a later session (the ledger already has a plan line naming the integration branch) that is not already detached at that branch's head runs `git switch --detach ` before `register`, whatever mode using-git-worktrees reported (an existing worktree, a native tool's worktree, or work in place); a worktree that skill created detached is already there. Before that detach, and before any claim, a later session compares `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` with the `at ` of every other session's newest session line: a match means you are inside another session's worktree (a native tool can resume one under the same name), so do not detach, switch or claim there. Leave it, create your own worktree with a name that carries your session id (using-git-worktrees, Detaching a later session), append a fresh session line from it, and detach that one. When the plan file lives in another repository than the code, pass `--code-repo ` to every `sdd-state` call; an omitted option means the current repository, and a wrong one is `wrong-repo`. - Quote the graph in the ledger: run `scripts/sdd-state deps PLAN_FILE` and append its lines after the scan table. The scan's conflict rows include `scripts/sdd-state deps --check PLAN_FILE --ledger /progress.md`'s lines: each `conflict tasks=A,B ...` is a row for your human partner, settled by an amendment (`scripts/sdd-state amend PLAN_FILE --from --base --message `, with `--accept 'tasks=A,B path=

'` when they accept the overlap; the edited copy is a file outside the checkout's plan path, a copy in the plan's workspace, never the checked-out plan file itself, which `amend` refuses) and never by editing the plan in the worktree alone, because the plan ref is what every session reads. - The ledger is your recovery map: the commits it names exist in git even when your context no longer remembers creating them. After compaction, trust the ledger and `git log` over your own recollection. - The workspace is scratch for the working tree and a record on the branch: the Finish step removes the plan's directory through `scripts/sdd-state finish PLAN_FILE --session `, and the branch history keeps it, so an evidence note can cite `git show :plans//`. Nothing inside the checkout is reclaimed automatically; `scripts/sdd-state prune --repo

` lists and removes idle plan directories only when asked. Snapshot the workspace (`scripts/sdd-state snapshot PLAN_FILE`) after the pre-flight scan table and before the final review; `scripts/sdd-state complete` snapshots after every completion line it writes, so a hand-off or a crash loses at most the task in flight. The completion's durable record is the snapshot `complete` takes, so that helper's status line decides whether you go on: `status=complete` continues, `busy` and `error` are retried, and every other status stops. A snapshot you run by hand answers `snapshot` (or `plain`, where no state branch exists), which continues; `none` means what you just wrote is not in the workspace the helper sees, and `error` (exit 2) means the commit or the ref update failed; both stop until the snapshot succeeds. When your human partner asks to hand the run to another host, run `scripts/sdd-state handoff PLAN_FILE --push` (the only time the state branch is pushed, never on your own initiative), report its status line, relay `plan-not-committed` with the commands to commit the plan, relay `code-dirty` with the listed paths as a question (only an explicit yes passes `--code-dirty-ok`), relay `detached-head` by asking for a branch name and creating it in the repository the line names (`repo=code` or `repo=plan`: `git -C switch -c `) before retrying, relay `shallow-source` (exit 12) the same way (a full clone, or `git -C fetch --unshallow`, since a shallow code or plan repository cannot record a root), and stop on `plain` (exit 7: this host has no state branch, so there is no dossier to push), `scan-failed` (exit 5: the pre-push scan named in `hyperpowers.prePushScan` rejected the range; show its output and ask) and `push-failed` (exit 1: the remote moved or could not be reached; run `sync` first, then retry): none of them is a hand-off, so report nothing as ready to pull. `snapshot ... push=none` (exit 0) is no hand-off either: the plan repository has no remote, so the record is committed on this host and nothing left it; report it as a local snapshot and ask your human partner for a remote if the dossier has to travel. On `pushed`, list the branches named in `code=` and, when present, `plan=` for your human partner to push here and pull there. You push none of them unless asked. Read the plan once, note its context and Global Constraints, and create a todo per task where your harness surfaces todos — the ledger is the progress record either way; todos mirror it, never replace it. Read the plan's `**Spec:**` header and the spec file it names: the spec is the binding authority the plan argues from, and conflicts inside the plan resolve against it. A plan whose spec is `none` or unreachable gets a ledger line saying so — without a spec, a conflict has no tiebreaker but your human partner. When the plan has a spec, dry-run the decision compiler over it now: `bash /scripts/decisions-compile --dry-run` (the finishing-a-development-branch skill, `../finishing-a-development-branch/` relative to this one). Exit 0 confirms the spec's `## Decisions` list parses; its numbered listing goes into the ledger under a `Decisions listing:` line for the extractor's dispatch. Exit 2 for a missing list is the legacy-spec case: draft the list from the spec's own text, one item per decision it states, show it to your human partner, and write it into the spec once they approve it, committing that edit on the branch. Any other exit 2 names what to fix first (a spec that is not committed, or a `Supersedes:` problem) to resolve with them the same way. After any repair, run the dry run again until it exits 0, and only then write its numbered listing into the ledger. The session is at its start, so this costs no cycle time. When the plan has no spec (`none`, or unreachable, per the ledger line above), write `Decisions: none (no spec)` in the ledger and skip the listing, the extractor and the spec in the hand-off: finishing then takes its test-only path. Before dispatching Task 1, scan the plan once for conflicts, writing down what you checked as you check it: - tasks that contradict each other or the plan's Global Constraints - anything the plan explicitly mandates that the review rubric treats as a defect (a test that asserts nothing, verbatim duplication of a logic block) The scan's output is a table, not a verdict. One row for every pair of tasks that share a file or an interface: the two tasks, what one produces against what the other consumes, and what you found. One row for every task: whether its own text agrees with itself — the tests it specifies against the code it specifies, the files it creates against the files it later touches. "The scan is clean" without those rows is not a scan you ran. Write the table to the ledger. Then present everything it surfaced to your human partner as ONE batched question — each finding beside the plan text that mandates it, asking which governs — before execution begins, not one interrupt per discovery mid-plan. Each finding is a decision with consequences downstream, so it gets the shape the brainstorming skill's Deciding Together section describes: the conflict and what each resolution costs in chat, then the selection widget to collect the answers. If the scan is clean, proceed without comment. The review loop remains the net for conflicts that only emerge from implementation. ## Model Selection Match the model to the task's difficulty rather than defaulting. Two rules are defaults you will get wrong by omission, so they stay here: **always specify the model explicitly when dispatching a subagent** — an omitted model inherits your session's, usually the most capable and most expensive — and **a mid-tier model is the floor for reviewers and for implementers working from prose descriptions**, whatever the schedule pressure. The cheapest tier is for transcription, where the task's own text carries the complete code to write, and for single-file mechanical fixes. The per-role guidance, the complexity signals, and the fix-loop escalation rule are in [model-selection.md](model-selection.md). ## The Task Loop **Batch small same-shape work.** When the plan lists several tasks that are each a small, independent edit of the same kind — the same one-line fix, constant change, or field addition repeated across files — do not dispatch one subagent per task. Compose ONE dispatch brief listing every file and its change, send the whole batch to a single subagent, and review its diff as one unit. Reserve one-dispatch-per-task for work that needs its own judgment, its own tests, or its own review surface. A batch's effective risk tier for the per-task Codex gate is the MAX of the batched tasks' declared tiers — batching low-tier tasks never manufactures a gate skip. Everything you paste into a dispatch prompt — and everything a subagent prints back — stays resident in your context for the rest of the session and is re-read on every later turn. Hand artifacts over as files. **Waiting on subagents and long commands.** On Claude Code, wait in the foreground: - Dispatch implementer, task-reviewer, fix-round, re-review and final-reviewer subagents with `run_in_background: false`. Your next step always depends on the result, and a foreground call keeps your turn open, which is what an editor such as Zed shows as the session working. A background dispatch ends the turn while the subagent runs, and the editor shows the session idle. - Run a covering command expected to finish within 10 minutes in the foreground, with an explicit timeout of at least its expected runtime and at most 600000 ms. - A command that may run past 10 minutes is a tracked job. Allocate it in the foreground with `scripts/tracked-job new PLAN_FILE --budget-ms ` (the watch budget below; the helper writes the `jobdir=` line in the ledger itself), launch `scripts/tracked-job run -- ` through the tracked background option with the budget as its timeout, then watch it in the foreground with repeated `scripts/tracked-job wait --max-ms 600000` calls: `exited code=0` is success; any other `exited` code is a failed command, handled as that command's failure (a failed test is a fix round, a failed covering command a failed task); `running` at the bound means another `wait`; on `lost`, run `tracked-job stop ` first and read its answer before you go on: only `stopped` or `not-running` means the survivors are swept and the job can be treated as failed (a process in the job's group that carried no fence is left alone and counted as `skipped` in `/meta.json`, and one that outlived the KILL is counted in `survivors`; report a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped`, or a record you cannot read, to your human partner with the jobdir and pgid before you go on, and never call that job stopped); `busy` means the lock was held and nothing was swept, so run `stop` again; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it to your human partner naming the jobdir and leave the job live; `lost-unswept pgid=` means the sweep needs a shell that can list processes and read their identity (the sandbox cannot), so the job stays live to the stop guard until `tracked-job stop ` runs where it can: report it to your human partner with its pgid beside the failure, and expect a reused pid to read as `running` until that sweep. When you need a job's output, write the tail of its `out.log` to `/reports/job-.txt` and cite the path; output never goes in the ledger. A background shell you start in a turn without `tracked-job` is live work no job record names: end the turn while one is still running and the stop guard refuses that turn end as `live-shell`. Codex reviews already follow this shape through the recipe's `status --wait --json` loop. - **Watch budget.** The total watch on one job is three times the plan's stated runtime for it, or 60 minutes when the plan states none, capped at the harness's maximum background lifetime (7200000 ms on Claude Code). The watch ends when `wait` reports `exited`, `lost` or `lost-unswept`; a supervisor the harness killed writes no exit file, and `wait` reports it as `lost`. When the budget is spent with the job still running, run `tracked-job stop ` and read its answer before you end the turn: `stopped` or `not-running` means the job is over, so write the `out.log` tail to `/reports/job-.txt` and report BLOCKED naming that path (a nonzero `survivors` or `skipped` in `/meta.json`, or a record you cannot read, is reported the same way, with the jobdir and pgid, and that job is never called stopped); `busy` means the workspace lock was held and nothing changed, so run `stop` again; `stop-timeout` means the supervisor has not concluded the job, so run `stop` again, three calls in all, and escalate a third one to your human partner as a job still live, naming the jobdir; `status=error` means the job directory could not be read, so escalate it the same way, naming the jobdir; `lost-unswept pgid=` leaves the job live, so report it to your human partner as still live with its pgid, never as stopped. On a harness whose subagents run asynchronously, never poll a wait interface with short timeouts, and never sit in one silent, open-ended wait either. While you have local work — ledger updates, packaging the next review, reading reports — keep working; child results arrive on their own. When you are genuinely idle, wait in bounded stretches (five to ten minutes, where your platform allows), and between stretches post one line of status and reconcile your live children: list them, and chase any that finished without reporting. A bounded stretch keeps nearly all of a long wait's efficiency while guaranteeing a stuck or lost child is noticed within minutes, not at the end of the session. Codex's `wait_agent` blocks inside the turn; `using-hyperpowers/references/codex-tools.md` maps it. ### 1. Dispatch the implementer Record BASE right after `git switch ` and before dispatching, as the task branch's fork point from the integration branch: `git merge-base HEAD refs/heads/` (the full ref name, so a tag with the branch's name cannot be read instead). On a fresh claim that is the claim's `from=` commit. On a takeover it is the original claim's base, or, once the conflict route has merged the integration branch into the task branch, the integration head merged in; the previous holder's commits stay in the review package and the fix-round diffs either way, which both need BASE. A HEAD read before the claim can lag the integration branch while other sessions merge. - **Task brief:** before dispatching an implementer, run this skill's `scripts/task-brief PLAN_FILE N` — it extracts the task's full text to a uniquely named file and prints `wrote : lines`. Take the path from that line; do not paste the line itself into a dispatch. Compose the dispatch so the brief stays the single source of requirements. Your dispatch should contain: (1) one line on where this task fits in the project; (2) the brief path, introduced as "read this first — it is your requirements, with the exact values to use verbatim"; (3) interfaces and decisions from earlier tasks that the brief cannot know; (4) your resolution of any ambiguity you noticed in the brief; (5) the report-file path and report contract. Exact values (numbers, magic strings, signatures, test cases) appear only in the brief. Never make a subagent read the whole plan file. - **Report file:** name the implementer's report file after the brief (brief `…/task-N-brief.md` → report `…/task-N-report.md`) and put it in the dispatch prompt. The implementer writes the full report there and returns only status, commits, a one-line test summary, and concerns. - A dispatch prompt describes one task, not the session's history. Do not paste accumulated prior-task summaries ("state after Tasks 1-3") into later dispatches — a real session's dispatch hit 42k chars of which 99% was pasted history. A fresh subagent needs its task, the interfaces it touches, and the global constraints. Nothing else. - The dispatch carries the no-subagents contract (it is in the implementer template): the implementer never dispatches subagents — not helpers, and never a reviewer. Review arrives from you, after the report. In real sessions, every reviewer a worker spawned duplicated the task review the controller dispatched anyway — a full extra review seat per task. - Subagents follow hyperpowers:test-driven-development for the task's tests. - If an earlier task deferred a finding in the area this task touches — a Minor in the ledger, or one your human partner decided — carry a pointer to that ledger entry in the dispatch. - Ask what to take: `scripts/sdd-state next PLAN_FILE --session `. `status=next tasks=` names the claimable tasks in plan order, this session's own claims first; claim the first: `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE N --session `. `claimed` prints the task branch and its base: check the branch out (`git switch `) and dispatch on it; `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after compaction) prints the same two fields: check the branch out and proceed; `held` with `own=1` and `merged=1` means the task is already merged and its branch deleted: check nothing out and resume it at its completion line (Complete the task, below); `claimed` with `takeover=1` and `merged=1` means the same after a takeover: the task is already merged, so check nothing out, dispatch nothing, and resume it at its completion line (the previous holder's task branch may still exist; you do not need it); `held` from `claim` after `next` offered the task is a race lost, run `next` again; `blocked` means the plan moved under you, run `next` again. A task held by another session is ordinary while next offers another: take what it offers. When `next` prints `status=none reason=`: `complete` goes to the final train (Finish below); `assigned-complete` is reported and the session hands back; `held` and `blocked` mean post a waiting record (`scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --kind tasks --note ""`), print `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE`, and hand back with the board's session lines in your message. Take a held task over only on your human partner's explicit yes to a question that names the holder and the time since (`--takeover`), recording the takeover beside the original identity; `own-blocked` means an amendment put a prerequisite under your own claim: post, print the board, hand back, and let your human partner remove the edge or let the prerequisite complete. `done`, `no-workspace` and `error` keep their handling: `done`: another session completed the task since you read the ledger; read its completion line, mark the task done, and never dispatch it. `no-workspace` (exit 2): the workspace is gone (finished or pruned elsewhere); stop, run `sync`, and re-read the ledger before anything else. `error` (exit 2, the same exit as `no-workspace` and a different problem): a read or a write failed, and the claim may already have been published; only your own retry of the same claim (which then answers `held own=1`) or a takeover clears it. Stop, show the stderr line, and retry the same claim once its cause is fixed; `sync` is still not the answer. Any other status stops the dispatch until `claim` succeeds; show its stderr line. - Record the implementer's agent identity from the dispatch result in the ledger's task entry (`Task : implementer (model , session , worktree , branch )`) — fix-loop rounds 1-3 resume this agent where the harness has no foreground dispatch and dispatch on its recorded model where it does, and after compaction the ledger is the only place the identity survives once its agent has exited. An identity that was never written down forces a fresh takeover where a resume was owed. - When another session may be live on this plan, append ledger lines with a quoted heredoc (`cat >> /progress.md <<'EOF'`), never with the Edit tool, whose read-modify-write drops a line another session appended in between. - One implementer at a time in this session: parallel work is other sessions' (one controller per task branch); never dispatch two implementers at once here. - Where the Agent tool offers `run_in_background`, dispatch with it false; where it does not (fork mode in an interactive terminal), dispatches run in the background and the stop guard treats them as live work. Template: [implementer-prompt.md](implementer-prompt.md) ### 2. Handle the report **Subagent Reports Are Claims.** Subagent reports are claims, not evidence. Before acting on any completed-status report (DONE or DONE_WITH_CONCERNS) or a fix report — dispatching the reviewer, re-running a gate, marking a task complete — the controller re-runs the named covering test command directly and compares the output against the report. A misreported result is a failed task: re-dispatch with the discrepancy named, not a bookkeeping correction. Every implementer and fix dispatch names either its covering test command(s) or an explicit `no covering command: ` line plus the controller's substitute verification (read the diff against the brief; render or grep the changed doc). A dispatch naming neither is malformed — fix the dispatch, not the rule. A covering command must be able to fail. One that can no-op on the state under test — a changed-files linter on a clean tree, a test filter that matches nothing — is not covering evidence, however honestly it exits 0. Name the files or the test ids explicitly so the command exercises what the report claims. Implementer subagents report one of four statuses. Handle each appropriately: **DONE:** Generate the review package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD`, from this skill's directory — it prints `wrote : commit(s), bytes`, so take the path from that line; BASE is the commit you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently drops all but the last commit of a multi-commit task). If `review-package` exits non-zero, read its stderr and fix the range before dispatching — exit 2 means bad inputs (wrong argument count, a missing plan file, a ref that does not resolve) or an ancestry check git itself could not answer (a missing or corrupt object); exit 3 means BASE..HEAD is empty or HEAD is not a descendant of BASE, usually a wrong-branch commit; never dispatch a reviewer without a package. Otherwise, dispatch the task reviewer with the path. **DONE_WITH_CONCERNS:** The implementer completed the work but flagged doubts. Read the concerns before proceeding. If the concerns are about correctness or scope, address them before review. If they're observations (e.g., "this file is getting large"), note them and proceed to review. **NEEDS_CONTEXT:** The implementer needs information that wasn't provided. Provide the missing context and re-dispatch. **BLOCKED:** The implementer cannot complete the task. Assess the blocker: 1. If it's a context problem, provide more context and re-dispatch with the same model 2. If the task requires more reasoning, re-dispatch with a more capable model 3. If the task is too large, break it into smaller pieces 4. If the plan itself is wrong, stop and escalate to your human partner — the plan text, what it breaks, and the correction you would make **Never** ignore an escalation or force the same model to retry without changes. If the implementer said it's stuck, something needs to change. If the implementer asks questions — before starting or mid-task — answer clearly and completely, provide additional context if needed, and don't rush it into implementation. ### 3. Review the task Per-task reviews are task-scoped gates. The broad review happens once, at the final whole-branch review. Never skip the task review, and never accept a report missing either verdict — spec compliance AND task quality are both required. Implementer self-review never replaces the task review; both are needed. Note the task's effective risk tier as you go (see Risk Tiers, below) — the Claude task review always runs, but the tier decides whether step 4's per-task Codex gate does. - Hand the reviewer its diff as a file: run this skill's `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE BASE HEAD` — it prints `wrote : commit(s), bytes`, so take the path from that line and pass it to the reviewer (or, without bash: `git log --oneline`, `git diff --stat`, and `git diff -U10` for the range, redirected to one uniquely named file). The output never enters your own context, and the reviewer sees the commit list, stat summary, and full diff with context in one Read call. Use the BASE you recorded before dispatching the implementer — never `HEAD~1`, which silently truncates multi-commit tasks. Never dispatch a task reviewer without a diff file. - **Reviewer inputs:** the task reviewer gets three paths — the same brief file, the report file, and the review package — plus the global constraints that bind the task. Write those global constraints to a small file alongside the brief and report: the per-task Codex gate takes the same file as its global-constraints handoff. - The global-constraints block you hand the reviewer is its attention lens. Copy the binding requirements verbatim from the plan's Global Constraints section or the spec: exact values, exact formats, and the stated relationships between components ("same layout as X", "matches Y"). The reviewer's template already carries the process rules (YAGNI, test hygiene, review method) — the constraints block is for what THIS project's spec demands. - Do not add open-ended directives like "check all uses" or "run race tests if useful" without a concrete, task-specific reason - Do not ask a reviewer to re-run tests the implementer already ran on the same code — the implementer's report carries the test evidence - Do not pre-judge findings for the reviewer — never instruct a reviewer to ignore or not flag a specific issue. If you believe a finding would be a false positive, let the reviewer raise it and adjudicate it in the review loop. If the prompt you are writing contains "do not flag," "don't treat X as a defect," "at most Minor," or "the plan chose" — stop: you are pre-judging, usually to spare yourself a review loop. When the plan supplies example code, weaknesses in that code are fair review targets — the example was a starting point, not evidence that its weaknesses were chosen. The task reviewer may report "⚠️ Cannot verify from diff" items — requirements that live in unchanged code or span tasks. These do not block the rest of the review, but you must resolve each one yourself before marking the task complete: you hold the plan and cross-task context the reviewer lacks. If you confirm an item is a real gap, treat it as a failed spec review — it enters the fix loop with the other findings. Template: [task-reviewer-prompt.md](task-reviewer-prompt.md) ### 4. The fix loop The loop triggers when the review reports spec ❌, any Critical or Important finding, a ⚠️ item you confirmed as a real gap, or a blocking finding from the per-task Codex gate below. Task-reviewer findings are claims too. The fixing implementer verifies each finding against the code before fixing it (hyperpowers:receiving-code-review); a finding is declined only as refuted or corrected with file:line evidence, which the controller records in the ledger; a confirmed finding is fixed or carried open; a finding nobody can settle stays open and counts against the round cap. Before the loop starts, two routes leave it immediately: - Record Minor findings in the progress ledger as you go (`Task : minor (deferred): `), and point the final whole-branch review at that list so it can triage which must be fixed before merge. A roll-up nobody reads is a silent discard. Minor findings never enter the loop. - A finding labeled plan-mandated — or any finding that conflicts with what the plan's text requires — is your human partner's decision: present the finding and the plan text beside it and ask which governs. Do not dismiss the finding because the plan mandates it, and do not dispatch a fix that contradicts the plan without asking. Everything else enters the loop — the Claude task reviewer's blocking findings and the per-task Codex gate's blocking findings alike. They are ONE loop with ONE shared cap of **five rounds per task**: the gate does not run a count of its own. A fix round is one fix dispatch — or one controller-applied de-minimis fix — plus one scoped re-review. **Rounds 1-3 — the same model, carrying the task's record.** Where the Agent tool offers `run_in_background` (Claude Code outside fork mode), dispatch a fresh implementer in the foreground (`run_in_background: false`) with the brief path, the report-file path, and the open findings verbatim, on the original implementer's model (the `model` in its ledger identity line); tell it a prior implementer did the task and the report file records what it did and tried. A foreground dispatch keeps your turn open until the fix returns, so a fix round on Claude Code dispatches a fresh foreground implementer; a SendMessage resume is for harnesses without the option, Claude Code's fork mode among them. On those harnesses, resume the original implementer with the findings verbatim: its context is intact. If the harness cannot message a live subagent either, dispatch a fresh implementer with the brief path, the report-file path, and the findings; the report file is the persistent memory either way. **Rounds 4-5 — dispatch a fresh takeover implementer on a more capable model** (per Model Selection), with the brief path, the report-file path, the open findings, and this framing: "A prior implementer attempted this task [N] times; you own it now. Read the report file for what was tried." A loop that survives three rounds usually means the same model cannot see its own problem: the takeover brings a more capable one. **Every round, either way:** the implementer fixes, re-runs the tests covering the amended code, appends its fix report to the same report file, and returns the short contract. Before re-dispatching the reviewer, confirm the fix report contains the covering tests, the command run, and the output; dispatch the re-review once all three are present. That precondition covers the findings the round fixed; a round that declines every finding is defined below. Name the covering test files in the fix message — a one-line fix does not need the whole suite. The per-task loop gives a fix round to an implementer rather than a fixer, so it never uses [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md) — that template belongs to the final review's one fix wave. **The re-review is scoped.** Run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` where FIX_BASE is the head the previous review saw, and dispatch [re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) with the findings list, the brief, the report file, and the printed diff path. The re-reviewer verdicts each finding ADDRESSED, NOT ADDRESSED, or DECLINED — a refuted or corrected finding whose file:line evidence the re-reviewer has confirmed; an unconfirmed decline stays NOT ADDRESSED — and flags new breakage in the fix diff only. The controller records each DECLINED finding in the ledger with its evidence. New Critical/Important breakage in the fix diff joins the open findings list. Out-of-scope observations go to the ledger as deferred minors — they never extend the loop. Every round in this loop ends with the scoped re-review — never a full task-reviewer re-run, whatever the finding's origin. **A round that declines every finding changes no code.** There is no fix diff and no covering test to confirm; the implementer's report is the artifact, carrying for each finding the refuted or corrected evidence at file:line. Skip `scripts/review-package` for that round — its range is empty — and dispatch the scoped re-review with the findings list, the brief, the report, and the previous review's package path, so the re-reviewer verdicts each finding DECLINED or NOT ADDRESSED from the evidence alone. The covering-tests precondition applies only to findings that were fixed. Record the round as `(0 addressed, declined, open)`; a NOT ADDRESSED verdict keeps that finding open and the round counts toward the cap as usual. **After each round,** append to the ledger: `Task : fix round /5 ( addressed, declined, open — ; commits ..)` Never fix findings yourself in the controller session — your context stays clean for coordination, and controller fixes skip review. One narrow exception: a fix fully specified by the finding itself — exact file, exact lines, exact replacement, no judgment left — touching at most 3 lines in one file with no new logic, may be controller-applied — one finding per reach; a round holding two such findings is not de minimis. The exception waives nothing else: it consumes a fix round and ends in the same scoped re-review; the controller applies the edit and runs the fix's covering command FIRST — a failure means the fix was not de minimis: revert the edit, spend no round, and go back to the round's own rule — then commits the verified fix (the re-review packages committed diffs — an uncommitted fix hands it nothing) and appends the fix report — the command, its output, and a diff summary — to the task's report file itself, exactly as an implementer would. Its ledger line keeps the fix-round schema with the marker inside it: `Task : fix round /5 controller-applied (de minimis) ( addressed, declined, open — ; commits ..)`. Reaching for it twice in the same task means the findings are not de minimis — go back to the round's own rule: hand the findings to an implementer at rounds 1-3, dispatch the takeover at rounds 4-5. **Codex Review Gate (Claude Code only).** When running under Claude Code, add a Codex **code** review gate at two points — here, per task, and once more at the final whole-branch review — following [../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md). Probe once per skill run and reuse the result; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice once and run both gates as no-ops. - **Per task:** after the task reviewer approves (spec ✅ and quality approved) and before marking the task complete, run the gate (standard/high effective tiers; an effective-low task skips it per Risk Tiers below, recording the tier-skip event instead) using the per-task code recipe with `--base `. Provide the task brief path, implementer report path, review-package path, and the global-constraints file you wrote in step 3. The gate's dossier `--adjudications` inputs carry the plan's `**Spec:**` file path beside any spec-gate ledger, so the reviewer is handed the binding authority instead of inferring it. - **Rounds are shared, not stacked.** Blocking findings from this gate enter the same five-round loop above, at the next round number — the gate has no separate Codex ceiling of its own. The task's fix-round budget is five, shared across Claude-reviewer rounds and Codex-gate rounds. Three mechanics keep that single budget honest: 1. **One `GATE_DIR` for this task's whole gate lifecycle.** Create it at the task's first gate invocation and reuse that same dir for every Codex re-round of this task — the gate doc's §3 contract, "Use one `GATE_DIR` for the whole gate." `gate-round`'s counter lives in that dir, so it counts exactly this task's gate rounds and nothing else. When the `GATE_DIR` is first created, record it in the progress ledger as one line `Task N gate dir: `; on resume (or any later Codex re-round), reuse the ledgered path instead of creating a new one; if the ledgered dir no longer exists (cache purged), treat the task's prior gate rounds as unknown and fail closed: do not assume zero — reconstruct the consumed-round count from the ledger's fix-round entries and, if gate rounds cannot be established, surface via BLOCKED rather than restarting the count. 2. **Let the counter do the arithmetic.** `gate-round` compares its LOCAL count — gate rounds only, monotonic within the `GATE_DIR` — against a ceiling, so the ceiling must leave gate rounds out; they are already in that count. Pass `--consumed ` (all fix/re-review rounds, whatever the finding's origin — the gate's own invocation rounds are excluded only because `gate-round`'s counter already holds them) and the script derives the ceiling from the shared five-round cap itself. Recompute the consumed count at each call: non-gate rounds may land between gate rounds. Do not hand-compute `--ceiling` for a task gate — that is how twenty measured task gates recorded ceilings of 1, 2, 6, and 7, two of which the cap makes impossible. `--consumed` cannot express them. 3. **A spent cap is BLOCKED, not a gate round.** When the task's consumed rounds already total five, `--consumed 5` yields a ceiling of zero and the gate backstops on its first call. That is the fail-closed floor, not the intended path: check before calling, and when the cap is spent follow the breaker below and surface the task as BLOCKED rather than spending a gate invocation to learn it. The invariant in one line: **local gate rounds + non-gate fix rounds ≤ 5**, enforced because `gate-round` blocks (verdict `backstop`) the moment its local count would exceed the ceiling. Count every round the gate runs against the task's shared budget — each gate round consumes one of the five, exactly like a reviewer round. After a Codex-triggered fix, the scoped re-review verifies it; the gate re-runs only once that re-review verdicts every finding ADDRESSED or DECLINED. **The breaker.** When round 5's re-review — or a per-task Codex gate at the spent cap — still leaves blocking findings open, stop dispatching. The task does not silently continue and nothing is parked on your own authority: surface the open findings to your human partner as BLOCKED, each with the rounds already spent, what was tried, and the evidence. Ledger it: `Task : BLOCKED at cap — `. They decide what happens next. ### 5. Complete the task When the review comes back clean — the task reviewer approved, every fix-loop finding is addressed or declined, and the per-task Codex gate approved or was skipped by tier — in this order, each step idempotent on a resume: - Append `Task : approved ` with the head the reviewers saw, written with `git rev-parse ` (every later approval of the same task appends a new line; the newest is what merges). merge-back compares the whole id, so a shortened id reads as no approval. - Merge back: `scripts/sdd-state merge-back PLAN_FILE N --session --commit `. `merged` continues (`already=1` on a resume means the ref was moved before the crash). `conflict paths=`: merge the integration branch into the task branch in your worktree (`git merge `), resolve through one implementer dispatch whose brief names the paths and both sides, re-run the task reviewer over the resolution and the task gate's re-review lens, append the new `approved` line, and retry. `checked-out` names a worktree or `lease:`: a final train holds the branch; post a `tasks` record and retry after it ends, or ask your human partner to move the checkout. `not-approved approved=` means your bookkeeping is behind: the commit you passed is not the task's newest `approved` line, so append the `approved` line for the head the reviewers saw (or pass that head) and retry. `blocked waiting=` (exit 7) means an amendment put a prerequisite under your claim after you took it, and merge-back enforces the edge: leave the `approved` line as it is, and never write a completion line for a task this session did not complete. Run `next` and take what it offers; on `own-blocked`, post, print the board and hand back as the `own-blocked` text above says. Retry merge-back once every waiting task has its completion line, or after your human partner removes the edge. `not-holder owner=` (exit 4) means the claim is no longer yours (after a takeover your human partner granted, that session holds it): stop and hand back with the line; never repair the ledger or take the claim back. - Detach at the merged head and drop the task branch: `git switch --detach ` then `git branch -d ` (its commits are on the integration branch now; a missing branch on a resume is fine). If `-d` refuses, the branch holds commits that were never approved or merged: keep it, do not force the delete, and hand back to your human partner with git's output. - Complete the task: run `scripts/sdd-state complete PLAN_FILE N --commits ..` and repeat it until it prints `status=complete` (`busy` and `error` are retried; `unknown-task` means the number is not a heading in the plan, `no-workspace` that the ledger is gone, and a usage error that the arguments are wrong: each of those stops you, not the loop). Its `snapshot=` is the completion's durable record. - Mark the todo complete (where you keep todos), and run `next`. A task whose ledger has a `merged` line and no completion line is resumed at the completion line, never redispatched. ## The waiting board Before you ask your human partner a question, hand back BLOCKED, meet an empty frontier (`held` or `blocked`), or stop on a merge conflict, post what you wait on: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --kind [--task N] --note ""`, and put the session lines of `scripts/sdd-state board PLAN_FILE` in what you write. When you resume, clear it: `scripts/sdd-state wait PLAN_FILE --session --clear`. The board is how your human partner finds the session that needs them among several; a session that holds a claim and posts nothing shows as quiet after half an hour, which is where they look for a permission prompt. ## Risk Tiers (per-task Codex gate applicability) Tiers are `low`, `standard`, `high`, declared per task in the plan. A task skips the per-task Codex gate only when all three hold: declared low, the plan's own Codex gate actually reviewed the plan, and no escalation trigger fired at any point during execution. That skip is recorded durably. An unreviewed low tier — plan gate skipped, degraded, or outcome unknown — executes as standard, and a task demoted that way runs the full train and records NO tier-skip event. The Claude task reviewer and the final whole-branch train never tier off. When any task did skip, write `tier-skips.md` in this plan's workspace; Final Review hands its path to the final reviewer and the final Codex gate. The escalation triggers, the fallback rules, and the exact ledger line shape are in [risk-tiers.md](risk-tiers.md) — read it before dispatching any task declared low. ## Final Review The final train is claimed. When `next` says `complete`, run `scripts/sdd-state claim PLAN_FILE final --session `: `claimed` means this session runs the final review, the final gate and Finish; `blocked` names tasks still open (claims without completion lines elsewhere: wait or ask); `held` with your own session id (`own=1`, a resume after compaction) means this session already holds the train: continue as its holder; `held` names the session that holds it, or `lease= plan=` when a sibling plan's final holds the branch: post a `tasks` record naming the holder, print the board, and hand back. The holder checks the integration branch out in its own worktree (`git switch `), the one time a session does so, and runs the review package, the final reviewer, the fix wave and the final Codex gate on it; its fix commits land on the integration branch directly, which the lease makes safe. Once you hold the train and have checked the integration branch out, the final whole-branch review gets a package too: run `scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD` (MERGE_BASE = the commit the branch started from, e.g. `git merge-base main HEAD`) — take the path from the `wrote : ...` line and include it in the final review dispatch, so the final reviewer reads one file instead of re-deriving the branch diff with git commands. Dispatch on the most capable available model (see Model Selection), using hyperpowers:requesting-code-review's [code-reviewer.md](../requesting-code-review/code-reviewer.md). Point it at the ledger's deferred-minor lines — and at `tier-skips.md`, if any task skipped its per-task gate — so it can triage which must be fixed before merge. If the final whole-branch review returns findings, dispatch ONE fix subagent with the complete findings list — not one fixer per finding. Compose the dispatch from [fix-subagent-prompt.md](fix-subagent-prompt.md). Per-finding fixers each rebuild context and re-run suites; a real session's final-review fix wave cost more than all its tasks combined. Then run exactly one scoped re-review of the fix wave (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE FIX_BASE HEAD` over the fix range, [re-review-prompt.md](re-review-prompt.md) using its Final-wave usage note). There is no second fix wave: anything the re-review leaves open — and any finding that conflicts with the plan's text — goes to your human partner with the evidence, as BLOCKED, when finishing-a-development-branch presents the options. **Dispatch the decision extractor.** When the ledger has a `Decisions listing:` line (and otherwise nothing), once the fix wave and its re-review are clean (or the final review returned no findings), take a scratch directory from `../requesting-code-review/scripts/codex-review-dir`, regenerate the full-branch package (`scripts/review-package PLAN_FILE MERGE_BASE HEAD`, so a fix wave's commits are in it) and copy it and `/progress.md` into it, and dispatch the extractor in the background, composed from `../finishing-a-development-branch/decision-notes-prompt.md` with those two copies, the plan, the spec, the `Decisions listing:` from the ledger, the index (`decisions/README.md` beside the spec's directory) when it exists, and `/decision-notes.md` as its output path. Record it in the ledger: `Decision extractor: -> /decision-notes.md`. The dispatch is complete only when that line is in the ledger: write it before any other tool call, because after a compaction it is the only record of the task id and the notes path, and without it a resumed controller can neither collect nor stop the extractor. The extractor reads nothing inside the workspace, so Finish may delete the workspace while it runs; finishing-a-development-branch collects it after the full suite and never waits for it, and neither do you. On a harness with no tracked background subagent, skip the dispatch and note it in the ledger. If a Codex final-gate fix changes code after the dispatch: stop the extractor (TaskStop); when the fix altered one of the spec's decisions, settle that first (show your human partner the change you would write into the `## Decisions` item, write and commit it on the branch with their approval; without it the item stands and the change is raised again at the menu); re-run the dry run and replace the ledger's `Decisions listing:`; regenerate the full-branch package and copy it, with the current `/progress.md`, into the scratch directory, replacing the earlier copies; compose the replacement dispatch from those copies; then dispatch the extractor again and replace the `Decision extractor:` line. **Codex Review Gate — final whole-branch (Claude Code only).** After the final code-reviewer subagent and its fix wave, and before hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, run the gate using the final whole-branch code recipe with `--base `. Provide the branch review-package path, plan or requirements path, the Minor findings ledger if present, and the tier-skip summary if any task skipped. The final dossier passes the plan's `**Spec:**` file as a `--doc` input beside the plan, and carries the tier-skip summary among its `--adjudications`. Resolve blocking findings with one fix subagent carrying the complete list, per this section's existing guidance, before finishing. After any Codex-triggered final-review fix, re-run the final code-reviewer before re-running the final Codex gate. Unlike the per-task gate, the final gate keeps a ceiling of its own: the gate's convergence stop-rule and per-gate backstop bound this loop (code gates use a code-gate backstop of 3 rounds). If the backstop is hit with unresolved blocking findings, surface them to your human partner rather than looping. ## Finish When the final whole-branch review is clean and its fixes are merged: 1. **Read your session line** from the ledger (its `mode`), and copy the ledger's `Decisions listing:` and `Decision extractor:` lines (or its skip reason) into the hand-off message you are about to send: the next step removes the ledger from the working tree, and hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch takes the mode, the plan, the spec and the extractor's task id and output path as its input. 2. **Finish the workspace** with `scripts/sdd-state finish PLAN_FILE --session `: it refuses with `open-claims` while any claimed task lacks a completion line (that is a plan not finished, not a reason for `--force`), and with `busy` (exit 3) when another session is writing the workspace or a copy from an interrupted removal sits beside it (report the stderr line, wait for the other session or ask your human partner about the copy, then run `finish` again); it also refuses with `live-jobs` while a tracked job it names is still live (run `tracked-job wait` on it, or `tracked-job stop` when the job is no longer wanted, then run `finish` again). `not-holder` or `no-final-claim` (exit 11): this session does not hold the final train; stop and hand back. Otherwise it removes the plan's directory, commits the removal to the state branch, and prints `last=`, the commit that still holds the dossier, `push=/` and `receipt=`, the durable copy of the ledger, the guard's log and the job records; record the receipt path in your closing message. A line reading `receipt=none staging=` means the record exists only under that staging path: name the path to your human partner in the closing message. A space in either path prints as `%20`, so decode it before you name the path. On the plain backend it prints `backend=plain` instead of `last=` and `push=`, and there is nothing to push. `none` means there was no workspace to remove, and `error` (exit 2) that the removal or its commit failed: any status other than `finished` stops Finish until the command succeeds; show its stderr line. 3. **Verify deletion** with `test ! -d ""` to confirm it is gone. The push command is `git -C push `, the checkout being the parent of the `plans/` directory `sdd-dir` printed; run it only if your human partner asks. 4. **Keep the lease through the branch action.** `finish` leaves the branch lease in place; hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch marks the branch closing before a merge and releases the lease after whichever option your human partner chose. Hand it the plan path and your session id for that. When the final ends with a hand-back instead, detach your worktree first (`git switch --detach`) and then release the lease yourself, as the last action: `scripts/sdd-state lease PLAN_FILE --release --session `. A clean finish that leaves the workspace behind is an INCOMPLETE finish — "keeping it for reference" is not an option; the repo's commits are the durable record. Sibling directories belong to other plans; leave them alone. `scripts/sdd-state prune --repo ` is the only other remover, and it runs only when asked. Use hyperpowers:finishing-a-development-branch, passing the mode from your session line. Hand it the plan and the spec, and the extractor's task id and output path when one was dispatched; when the dispatch was skipped, hand over the ledger's reason instead and say so, and finishing compiles without notes; when the plan has no spec, say that, and finishing runs its test-only path. A decision a Codex-gate fix altered was settled in Final Review before the re-dispatch. ## Common Rationalizations The excuses that show up mid-run and what is actually true: [common-rationalizations.md](common-rationalizations.md). Read it the moment you catch yourself justifying a shortcut. ## Example Workflow A complete worked run, dispatch through finish: [example-workflow.md](example-workflow.md).
